title: Thunderstorms and flash flood risk on final day of UK heatwave
content:
The heatwave impacting parts of the UK this week continues into Tuesday with a risk of thunderstorms in some parts.

Pershore in Worcestershire and Cavendish in Suffolk hit three consecutive days of heatwave threshold temperatures on Monday and it is expected more parts of southern and eastern England will reach heatwave criteria on Tuesday.

Amber and yellow heat health alerts, external are in effect across much of England until 09:00 BST Wednesday, with temperatures expected to reach more than 30C in some areas.

The intense heat will be short lived though as a change in the weather pattern is on the way from midweek.

title: Village sees 50 days without rain during summer heatwave
content:
As the extremely dry spell continues across much of England and Wales, a number of weather stations have smashed their previous longest periods without rain.

It comes after the driest July for England and Wales, external since Met Office records began 190 years ago.

Already Wales and most of England are in drought, with parts of eastern Scotland in significant water scarcity.

Despite some locations receiving rain this week, not enough fell in drought-hit areas to provide any meaningful relief.

These include Wisley in Surrey, which has notched up 52 consecutive dry days and Coningsby in Lincolnshire with 43 days of no rainfall.

title: More areas of UK likely to move into drought as fifth heatwave builds
content:
As the hot and dry weather continues for much of the UK, drought status could be declared in additional parts of England this week.

The Environment Agency (EA) has suggested that "several areas" of England could enter drought status as "public water supplies remain under increasing pressure with continued dry weather and high demand".

For the seventh consecutive week, less than 10mm of rain fell across the country, with east and south-east England seeing less than 1mm of rain, according to data from the agency's latest drought summary.

More than half of England and the whole of Wales are already under drought conditions.

Reservoir levels have continued to fall, with almost all across England below normal and five classed as 'exceptionally low', according to the EA.

Wisley in Surrey has gone more than 50 days without a drop of rain. Southern England is approaching two months without any notable rainfall.

Customers of South West Water were the latest to see a hosepipe ban introduced on Saturday.

There are now more than 20 million people in the UK living in an area where prolonged dry weather combined with heatwaves and high demand for water has led to restrictions on usage.

Update: A previous version of this story said that the UK had recorded 35 days of temperatures exceeding 30C, breaking the previous record. As of 9 August, the UK has equalled the 1995 record, with 34 days of temperatures exceeding 30C.

title: Brief relief ahead of fifth heatwave - as more areas could move into drought
content:
Much of the country will feel some relief from the heat early in the week before temperatures spike again.

On Monday, the air will feel a little fresher compared to the weekend with maximum temperatures in northern areas of the UK around 18 to 24C.

Further south, while cooler than Sunday, it will still be a very warm day with temperatures between 22 to 27C.

By Tuesday, warmer air will start to move back in across the UK with the highest temperatures across central southern England, the Midlands and east Wales.

Yellow heat-health alerts remain in force for much of England until 21:00 BST on Tuesday, though they are likely to be extended or upgraded as the heatwave nears.

Highs are likely to be around 27 to 30C.

Wednesday will see temperatures widely across England and Wales head into the high twenties and low thirties.

The peak of the extreme heat is set to arrive on Thursday, with temperatures reaching 36C (97F) in south-east England, and up to 35C likely across central and eastern England.

This would mark the fourth consecutive month where 35C has been reached in the UK – a new record.

Many locations will exceed their heatwave threshold of 25 to 28C – dependent on location – for the first day.

Some of the warmth will spread further north into northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland with temperatures into the low to mid-20s Celsius.

As heat builds throughout the week, overnight temperatures will stay relatively high bringing some uncomfortable nights for sleeping.

Minimum temperatures may not go lower than 16 to 18C across England and Wales.

There's also a possibility of a 'tropical night' – where temperatures remain above 20C all night – in south-east England.

title: Heatwave reveals lost archaeological sites across Wales
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
Lost archaeological sites have emerged in grasslands across Wales after a prolonged spell of hot and dry weather.

Wales has seen about 5% of the average rainfall for July, after a series of back-to-back heatwaves and a drier than usual April to June. A drought has also been triggered in parts of Wales.

Experts said these dry conditions have brought to light a range of hidden archaeological remains, including Roman buildings and practice trenches from World War One.

Many are only visible from the air as distinctive marks in crops and grass, with some not being seen for "two or three decades", according to the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (RCAHMW).

title: UK heatwave approaches two-week mark
content:
This year is already shaping up to be an extraordinary one for weather records in the UK, having broken those for monthly temperature in both May and June by more than two degrees.

This is the third heatwave of 2026. At the same point last year, we had also just seen the third heatwave of 2025. However, last July, some places in the south saw four consecutive days above 30C.

Heatwave conditions have also gripped parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland this week but the heat has been less intense and has not lasted as long.

Comparisons are being made with the historic hot summer of 1976. Whilst that year still holds the record for the longest heatwave, this year has seen higher extreme temperatures, and more "very hot days".

The dryness as well as the heat has been particularly notable. Some places in southern England such as Wisley in Surrey have seen no rainfall in 30 days.

Using Met Office HadUKP data on rainfall, there has been no rainfall recorded across the central England region for 15 days, the longest dry spell for 30 years.

Most of Wales and Northern Ireland have also had rainfall deficits, although parts of western Scotland have been wetter than average. That said, nowhere in the UK is currently in drought unlike the widespread one which accompanied the heatwave in 1976.

As well as the duration and frequency of the heatwaves of 2026 so far, it has been the intensity that has been remarkable.

This year has seen more days - six - in excess of 35C, and 35C has been recorded in three consecutive months (May, June and July) for the first time.

title: UK's most parched regions miss chance for rain ahead of next heatwave
content:
Amber heat health alerts have been issued for much of eastern England for later this week as temperatures rise again.

The East Midlands, East of England, London, and the South East are all under the amber alerts from 9am on Wednesday until 9am Thursday.

With the temperature forecast to peak in the mid-30s Celsius on Wednesday, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), which issues the alerts, warns that significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures.

Yorkshire and the Humber, the West Midlands, and the South West are all under less severe yellow alerts for the same period.

This latest heatwave comes after some of the driest regions of the UK missed their chance of rain over the weekend.

Parts of the northern and western UK saw some rainfall on Saturday and Sunday, with further showers and unsettled conditions expected over the next few days.

But southern parts of the country - where the least amount of rain has fallen - are set to see temperatures climb once again, with more dry and sunny weather in the forecast.

It comes as parts of Wales have officially entered drought status, while parts of southern, central and eastern England remain in "prolonged dry weather", the final stage before drought is declared.

The coming days will only exacerbate dry conditions as another heatwave is expected to be declared, with temperatures peaking around 34-35C (93-95F) in south-east England or the East of England.

title: Heatwave anxiety can make you feel 'incredibly helpless' - here's how to manage it
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
Watts is not alone. A 2022 study from the University of Bath estimates that about 4.6% of people in the UK have climate anxiety, which is recognised as a form of mental distress by professional bodies and the NHS. Young people and women are among the groups most at risk, according to a study published in 2025.

"Anticipatory anxiety", related to heatwaves in particular, has become more common, say psychologists Dr Caroline Hickman from the University of Bath and Dr Emma Lawrance from the University of Oxford.

"Once people have been through a traumatic event like a flood or a heatwave, they anticipate the next one," Hickman, who offers therapy to individuals experiencing climate anxiety, told the BBC.

In the UK, "now we're getting the repeat, repeat, repeat [heatwaves]. It triggers that sense that 'I can't be safe in the world, and the world can't be trusted'," she added.

In June's heatwave, Hickman said she "had people saying they're going to kill themselves, I've had people saying they're going to terminate pregnancies, I've had people saying that they want to sell their houses and move somewhere cooler".

Watts said that her video "clearly struck a chord with people" - including therapists posting comments about coping mechanisms - and that she wanted to help others deal with climate anxiety.

"It can go one of two ways. You can either just fall into doomism and think, 'What is the point?'" she said.

"Or you can try to do something. I sign petitions during a heatwave; I organise climate community events; I run a free children's clothes swap shop. During the last heatwave, I finally became vegetarian, because then I can tell my kids at least I tried."

title: Before-and-after satellite images show the staggering toll of France's worst wildfire season on record
author: Talia Lakritz
content:
Weeks of record-breaking heat and fast-moving wildfires have scorched large swaths of France.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said in a statement on Friday that 116,085 hectares of land had burned in wildfires across France this year, amounting to the country's worst wildfire season on record.

Around 250,000 people have been evacuated in the affected areas of the Gironde and Landes regions of southwest France since the wildfires began in mid-July, France's Interior Ministry said.

Record-breaking heat waves across Europe and prolonged drought conditions have contributed to the severity of the damage.

Photos show plumes of smoke visible from space, burned remains of neighborhoods, and France's continued firefighting efforts.

title: Nearly 3,000 heat-related deaths during summer heatwaves, UKHSA estimates
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
England is on track this year for the highest number of heat-related deaths since records began, according to estimates by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

In a preliminary assessment, it said there were an estimated 2,877 heat-related deaths during the May and June heatwaves, almost double the figure for the whole of last year.

An estimated 753 deaths were associated with the 24-27 May heatwave and a further 2,124 with the one from 21-28 June. Definitive figures are expected in early 2027.

Both spells broke Met Office UK monthly temperature records, with 35.1C (95.2F) recorded at Kew Gardens on 26 May and 38.0C recorded at Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.

The current record for heat-related deaths was set in 2022, when 2,985 deaths were recorded.

Report author Dr Ross Thompson, from the UKHSA, said "while the figures are interim, they suggest that, if we experience more periods of hot weather this summer, we could see the highest number of heat-associated deaths on record".

Thompson added: "These figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people's health.

"This is particularly true for those who are more vulnerable including older adults and people with underlying medical conditions."

He said "as the climate becomes warmer, we can expect periods of hot weather to become longer, more frequent and more extreme", adding that it is vital the country is prepared to deal with higher temperatures.

Earlier this week parts of the UK sweltered through another heatwave that peaked on Wednesday, with temperature reaching 35.2C in Writtle, Essex.

Cooler conditions and some rain are on the way for some on Thursday and into the weekend, but likely not in the driest areas.

title: DeepMind Says Its AI Can Predict Hurricanes Earlier Than Everyone Else
author: Victoria Turk
content:
In October 2025, a storm brewed over the Caribbean Sea. Weather models differed on its trajectory. Would it remain weak and end up in Haiti, or would it intensify and head to Jamaica? Artificial intelligence model WeatherNext, developed by Google’s DeepMind and Google Research, went with the latter. Five days before landfall, it predicted with 80 percent confidence that the storm system would hit Jamaica as a Category 5 hurricane.

Hurricane Melissa was catastrophic, causing flooding and landslides across Jamaica. But the AI model helped forecasters give an earlier warning to communities in its path, so they could better prepare.

In a paper published on Thursday in Nature, researchers show that the WeatherNext AI model can predict cyclones with unprecedented accuracy. On average, it gives forecasters a day more lead time than existing models; this means its predictions three days out are as accurate as previous models’ predictions two days out. On the ground, that extra day can mean a lot.

“Even a few hours can make a difference,” says Mike Brennan, director of the US National Hurricane Center. Organizing evacuations, staging supplies, and moving resources to respond to a hurricane risk are all time-sensitive tasks—and making the wrong decision can have big consequences. “Time is really golden when it comes to those types of decisions, so the ability to push forecast accuracy out as much as a day beyond what we've previously been able to do is really valuable,” he says.

Historically, bringing forecasts forward by a day would take a decade of work, the researchers say.

Modeling extreme events can be challenging for AI. Machine learning requires ample training data in order to make future predictions, but extreme events are by nature rare occurrences. “We don’t have that much cyclone data, but we have a lot of weather data,” says Ferran Alet, a research scientist at Google DeepMind and one of the paper’s lead authors. “So what we did was train a model to be both good at weather as well as cyclones.”

Hurricanes are particularly difficult to predict because they operate at multiple spatial scales, says Kate Musgrave, tropical cyclone group lead at the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere, and an author on the paper. Predicting a storm’s track—which direction it’s traveling—requires data about weather on a global scale, taking in information such as the location of cold fronts and prevailing winds. Predicting a storm’s intensity, however, requires much smaller-scale data focused specifically on the local atmospheric and ocean conditions.

“That’s something we just don’t get from these global models,” Musgrave says. While earlier AI models have done well at predicting a storm’s track, “intensity they could not do well at all.”

It’s critical to predict both: A change in intensity can mean the difference between a relatively weak storm and a major hurricane. Sometimes—as in the case of Hurricane Melissa—a storm system can intensify rapidly, developing into an emergency situation overnight. Melissa marked the first time the National Hurricane Centre was able to predict a Category 5 hurricane when the storm was only at a Category 1 stage.

Before the WeatherNext model was used in live forecasts, researchers tested it on retrospective data. “The results were so good that we were skeptical that we would actually see that in the real-time demonstration,” Musgrave says. But when forecasters started adopting the model into their operations, this performance held true. “I think everybody was surprised at just how well it did,” Musgrave says.

Even the DeepMind researchers working on the model don’t fully understand how the AI model produces such accurate predictions, given that it uses much lower-resolution atmospheric data than traditional models require to forecast storm intensity. “When we told the community that our model was only using relatively coarse resolution, they were shocked, because that means that the lower-resolution inputs capture more signal about what’s going to happen than previously believed,” Alet says.

title: France braces for fourth major heatwave as crews tackle Bordeaux blaze
content:
By Yves Herman and Janis Laizans

BORDEAUX, France, July 28 (Reuters) - France was bracing for its fourth major heatwave of the year on Tuesday, as soaring temperatures ‌and tinder-dry conditions across the southwest piled pressure on crews battling a giant ‌wildfire in the Bordeaux region.

Temperatures in Bordeaux are forecast to reach 33 degrees Celsius (91 degrees Fahrenheit) during the day, ​around 7 degrees above the average high between 1961 and 1990, according to the Reuters Climate Monitor.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The situation we are dealing with today is the most severe we have ever recorded, the toughest since the Second World War," President Emmanuel Macron, who flew to the area, said on ‌Monday evening.

Fire crews had contained ⁠the blaze overnight, but the situation remained difficult, Nathalie Delattre, Senator for Gironde, which covers the city of Bordeaux, said.

"Everything will depend on how ⁠the firefighters on the ground get on," she told BFM TV on Tuesday.

France is going through an unprecedented wildfire season. The area burned has already surpassed the previous record year of 2022.

The Landes ​area, southwest ​of Bordeaux, is covered by pine forests, which ​become highly flammable when dry. The ‌fire has burned down 42,000 hectares so far.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Authorities have evacuated about 220,000 people, including holidaymakers and local residents.

In the area of Biscarrosse, a town about 40 km south, which was hit by another wildfire last week, the situation has improved and some 15,000 evacuated people were gradually allowed back home in the town and a campsite nearby, the local administration said ‌on X.

"However, (the favourable) development does not mean the risk ​has been eliminated. Flare-ups remain possible, particularly due to ​weather conditions (wind, drought, etc.)," it said.

Temperatures ​were set to increase in the region from the afternoon and peak ‌at 37 degrees Celsius on Wednesday, weather ​office Meteo France said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Beyond ​the Gironde, French authorities have jailed a person in connection with wildfires in the Var area that firefighters are still battling, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez wrote in a ​post on social media platform ‌X.

Nunez said that 184 people have been detained since the beginning of the ​wildfire season.

(Reporting by Yves Herman, Manuel Ausloos, Inti Landauro, Sarah Meysonnier; additional reporting ​by Charlotte van Campenhout; Editing by Andrew Heavens)

title: Thousands in France allowed to return home as Europe tackles wildfires and heatwave
author: Eleanor Beardsley Robbie Griffiths
content:
Thousands in France allowed to return home as Europe tackles wildfires and heatwave

toggle caption Emma Da Silva/AP

BORDEAUX, France — Firefighters in southwestern France said Friday they were working on four active hotspots as they tried to put out fires that ripped through 100,000 acres of forest, villages and farmland over the past week.

Lt. Col. Eric Pitault, the spokesman for firefighters in the Gironde region, said that while the situation had "stabilized," there are still several zones that are difficult for responders to access.

He said authorities were hoping to have full control by the weekend.

Tens of thousands of people near Bordeaux who were evacuated due to fire risk were allowed to return to their homes on Thursday night, as the rest of Europe continued to tackle a historic heatwave.

"It's the first somewhat optimistic day," said Sophie Brocas, prefect of Bordeaux's Gironde region, as she allowed the 84,000 evacuees to return home. Some 60,000 had been allowed to return to their homes on Tuesday, according to the Associated Press.

Sponsor Message

"Our feeling is that we're getting back to the path of a normal life," Brocas added.

Some of these evacuations were preemptive. Authorities said there are no known civilian casualties. However, two firefighters lost their lives battling a forest fire near Bordeaux-Merignac Airport earlier in July.

Despite thousands being allowed to return home, many people remain in temporary shelters, including the Bordeaux convention center, which NPR visited this week.

Among the 6,000 people – and their many pets – taking shelter was 90-year-old Marie Lalana, who told NPR that she had fled her home so quickly that she forgot everything she needed, including her teeth, glasses and hearing aids.

Aurélien Costes, a scientist with the San José State University, told NPR that this year's intense fires in France have resembled similar blazes in California, saying they are likely to become more frequent as temperatures rise.

"You can have downdrafts that are very intense, and so when the downdrafts hit the ground, they can form winds that are going in any direction," Costes said. "This makes the fire behavior very erratic so it's very hard for the firefighters to anticipate what the fire is doing."

Another wildfire in the southeastern town of Brignoles this week forced hundreds of people to evacuate, including Hollywood actor George Clooney, his wife, Amal, and their children, according to the Associated Press.

toggle caption Emma Da Silva/AP

Heatwave across Europe

The fires in France are part of an unusually long spate of hot weather across Europe, which scientists from World Weather Attribution say have created conditions that make wildfires more likely across the continent.

Sponsor Message

This week, thousands of people were evacuated from the Greek island of Crete as fires burned on the south coast, according to the Associated Press. On Wednesday, two firefighters died on the island, while a third firefighter died battling a separate blaze on the Greek mainland.

In Germany, firefighters using drones and helicopters battled a forest fire near the Austrian border, according to the Associated Press, while in Turkey, responders tackled forest fires in four western provinces.

In England, firefighters worked to contain a fire near a nuclear power plant on Britain's east coast. The blaze, in the county of Suffolk, broke out on Wednesday afternoon, and quickly grew to over 350 acres, just three miles away from Sizewell B nuclear power station.

Over 100 firefighters and a helicopter were sent to tackle the flames, and late on Thursday night, authorities said the situation was stabilizing.

Earlier this week, the Environment Agency declared that half of England was in drought, due to a combination of weeks of very low rainfall and high temperatures. Rivers are running low, wildfire risk is increasing, and millions of people are living under restrictions over how much water they are allowed to use in their homes, the agency said.

On Thursday, Hungary Prime Minister Péter Magyar said officials would shut down the country's only nuclear power plant due to record low water levels in the nearby Danube River. The river's water is usually used to cool the plant.

Similarly, Romania shut down both reactors at its Cernavoda nuclear power plant, also citing low water levels in the Danube River that is used to cool them, according to Reuters.

The effects of climate change

On Friday, a network of scientists who use weather observations and climate models to understand how climate change influences the intensity and likelihood of extreme weather events said that climate change had contributed to recent fires in France and Spain.

Sponsor Message

In a new study, World Weather Attribution said that human-induced climate change made the fire-prone conditions at least twice as likely in southwestern France and at least 20 times as likely in central Spain.

title: Latin American governments prepare for El Nino as drought, floods and heat loom
content:
BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — Governments across Latin America are mobilizing firefighters, activating contingency plans and preparing water, energy and transportation systems as El Nino strengthens across the Pacific, raising concerns about drought, extreme heat, flooding and other climate-related disruptions in the months ahead.

The preparations come as meteorologists warn that El Nino is already underway and increasingly likely to strengthen through the remainder of the year. Unlike hurricanes or earthquakes, the climate phenomenon develops gradually over months, which gives governments time to prepare before its most severe impacts arrive.

But experts say authorities across the region have often struggled to turn forecasts into action, raising questions about whether countries will be better prepared than during previous El Nino events that caused widespread economic damage and disrupted water, energy and food systems.

Advertisement Advertisement

"Now is the time for decisions, for effective preparedness and the political consistency to really be proactive this time," said Rodney Martinez, the World Meteorological Organization's representative for North America, Central America and the Caribbean.

"El Nino is confirmed. El Nino is ongoing. It's not simply a possibility," he said.

Many countries have stepped up preparations

Previous strong El Nino events have caused billions of dollars in damage across Latin America, contributing to severe drought in some regions while triggering floods and landslides in others. The phenomenon has disrupted agriculture, strained drinking water supplies, fueled wildfires and, in some countries, reduced hydroelectric power generation, leading to energy shortages.

Martinez said countries should use the months before impacts intensify to secure alternative energy sources, protect vulnerable communities and prepare for potential strain on public services.

Advertisement Advertisement

In hydropower-dependent countries such as Ecuador, that could mean bringing thermal power generation online to offset lower reservoir levels during drier conditions and completing maintenance and procurement work well in advance. He pointed to Ecuador's energy crisis last year, when drought depleted water levels at hydroelectric facilities and contributed to widespread power outages.

Central America, parts of the Caribbean and northern South America are already experiencing drier-than-normal conditions associated with the phenomenon, according to the WMO. Those conditions are expected to expand into parts of the Amazon basin, raising concerns about water availability, agriculture and wildfire risk.

The threats vary considerably across the region.

In Brazil, Colombia and parts of Central America, authorities are focused on drought, water shortages and wildfire risk. Brazil has hired more than 4,600 federal personnel for wildfire prevention and response, expanded firefighting brigades and deployed aircraft ahead of what officials fear could be a difficult fire season. Colombia has activated water-monitoring systems, strengthened wildfire preparedness and urged local authorities to prepare for potential shortages.

Advertisement Advertisement

Elsewhere, governments are preparing for flooding. Ecuador, where strong El Nino events have historically brought damaging rains to the Pacific coast, has ordered local governments to develop contingency plans and allocated millions of dollars for flood mitigation, emergency response and agricultural recovery. Local authorities have begun clearing drainage channels, stabilizing hillsides and preparing emergency shelters.

Costa Rica says it has launched more than 200 measures under a national contingency plan, including efforts to protect water supplies, expand renewable energy generation and prepare for a potentially severe wildfire season. In Peru, authorities have strengthened monitoring and early-warning systems while expanding meteorological observation networks.

Panamanian authorities have developed plans to address potential impacts on operations at the Panama Canal, where lower rainfall can affect water availability needed to maintain shipping traffic through one of the world's most important trade routes.

The WMO official warned that drought and heat could threaten food security across parts of Central America's Dry Corridor while increasing wildfire risks in several countries. In areas expected to receive excessive rainfall, flooding can damage infrastructure, contaminate water supplies and increase the risk of disease outbreaks.

Advance warning does not always translate into action

Colombia's environment minister, Irene Vélez, told The Associated Press that El Nino is not new, but "what is new is its intensity. And because of that intensity, what is also new is how long it could last and the area it could affect."

Advertisement Advertisement

Despite the advance warning, Martinez said preparations remain uneven across the region.

"The reality is that this preparation doesn't happen until they have the emergency," he said.

Martinez said some authorities continue to delay decisions despite increasingly strong forecasts, either waiting for additional confirmation or assuming their countries will avoid the worst impacts. He warned that postponing decisions despite increasingly strong scientific evidence could leave governments scrambling to respond once droughts, floods and heat waves intensify.

Recent studies examining previous major El Nino events found their economic impacts can linger for years and ultimately cost the global economy trillions of dollars.

Advertisement Advertisement

His message to governments still waiting to act was simple.

"Be prepared in advance, in a serious way," Martinez said. ""The information is there. Now is the time for decisions."

Vélez said the challenge extends beyond responding to a single climate event and requires governments to adapt to increasingly extreme conditions.

"Climate change is here to stay," she said.

title: One of NASA’s Most Important Deep Space Observatories Hit by Spanish Wildfires
author: Brian Kahn
content:
Climate change has now become a problem for the whole solar system. On Friday, wildfires in Spain overran one of three observatories the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration uses to connect with spacecraft, including Voyager 1, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the recently completed Artemis mission around the Moon.

Spain declared a wildfire emergency as multiple blazes burned out of control near Madrid, with evacuation orders in place for 60,000 people. The affected area includes Robledo de Chavela, a municipality near the Deep Space Communications Complex run by NASA.

Dramatic images captured by news photographers showed the radio telescopes surrounded by smoke and fire. A NASA spokesperson said in an email to WIRED that the agency successfully evacuated all personnel.

They added that while the fire has now passed through the observatory complex, it remains unclear what impact the flames may have had on the sensitive equipment inside. “Any potential damage will be assessed when it is safe to do so,” the spokesperson said. They add that if conditions allow, a site assessment could happen as soon as Saturday.

For now, NASA said it has “seamlessly transitioned support for mission operations to the Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex in California, ensuring continuity of service and uninterrupted support for spacecraft communications.”

The facility in Spain, along with the others in Canberra, Australia, and Goldstone, California, make up what NASA calls the “largest and most sensitive scientific telecommunications system in the world.” The network allows NASA to transmit information from Earth to spacecraft, including the most distant human-made object in our solar system, Voyager 1. It’s also used to transfer data from the James Webb Space Telescope and send commands to other space vehicles. Oh, and the sites also contribute to radio astronomy observations. Suffice to say, it’s a very important collection of instruments for understanding the solar system.

Spain is far from the only country facing a wildfire crisis. Blazes are also burning out of control in France, where beachgoers saw skies turn orange and waves of ash washing ashore as firefighters worked to stop flames from spreading into the eponymous capital of the Bordeaux wine region.

“We learned in the middle of the afternoon that, following the wind shift, it had become a large, self-sustaining fire that is extremely difficult to bring under control,” French interior minister Laurent Nunez told national television channel Tf1. “It is now moving east, toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area. We are going to reorganize our response so we can fight it from the ground and prevent it from advancing.”

Roughly 200,000 people have been told to evacuate across the two countries.

Europe has seen record high temperatures this summer, driven by repeated heat domes camping over the continent and the UK, as well as climate change. Hot weather can dry out vegetation, priming forests to burn when hit by an errant spark. Similar stories have played out in other parts of the world recently, from Ontario, Canada, to the US Pacific Northwest.

Cooler weather is expected to arrive in the Mediterranean over the weekend, which should help firefighters get a handle on the blazes. But the respite will be short: Temperatures are expected to shoot up again on Monday and keep climbing throughout the week, eventually reaching up to 10 degrees Celsius (18 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal. That could worsen any wildfires in Spain or France that may still be burning—or help spark new ones.

title: Apple Donating to Japan Earthquake Relief Efforts
author: Juli Clover
content:
Apple CEO Tim Cook today said Apple would be making a donation to support earthquake relief efforts in Japan.



A magnitude 6.8 earthquake (per the USGS) hit the Kumamoto prefecture on Kyushu island on Tuesday, collapsing buildings and killing at least 34 people.

Japan has a very special place in my heart. We're thinking of everyone as they continue to face the effects of the Kumamoto earthquake and aftershocks. We're grateful to the first responders helping those in need. Apple is making a donation to support relief efforts. — Tim Cook (@tim_cook) July 30, 2026

Aftershocks continued on Wednesday and Thursday. Kyushu is the third largest of Japan's four main islands, and it has the second-highest population.

Apple often donates to the Red Cross for relief efforts during natural disasters, but donation amounts are not shared. Last night, Cook said Apple was donating to wildfire relief efforts in France, Spain, and other countries.

Kumamoto was previously hit with a deadly earthquake in 2016, and Apple collected donations for Japan through iTunes.

title: Spain's largest wildfire of the year burns for a fifth day as new heatwave looms
content:
MADRID, July 20 (Reuters) - A wildfire raged out of control across Spain's central Guadalajara province on Monday, burning for a fifth ‌day and becoming the largest blaze of the year, as forecasters ‌warned an approaching heatwave would raise fire risks across much of the country.

Spain and southern ​Europe are facing increasingly severe wildfire seasons, a trend scientists have linked to climate change.

The fire comes less than two weeks after a wildfire near Bedar, in Almeria province, killed 13 people - one of Spain's deadliest blazes in decades.

Advertisement Advertisement

Authorities ‌evacuated three additional municipalities ⁠on Monday as the La Mierla wildfire in Guadalajara province expanded to more than 26,000 hectares. More than 1,000 residents ⁠have been evacuated from their homes.

Regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said nearly 30 population centres were surrounded by the blaze, underscoring the challenge facing firefighters. Protecting lives ​and ​preventing the fire from reaching homes and ​urban areas remained the top ‌priority, he said.

Spain's weather agency AEMET said the heatwave, the third of 2026, was expected to last at least until Thursday, bringing temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) across much of the southeastern interior and pushing wildfire danger to extreme levels.

Some areas could reach 42 to 44 C ‌by Thursday as hot, dry air moves north ​from Africa. The agency also warned of ​possible dry thunderstorms in mountainous ​areas of eastern Spain.

Advertisement Advertisement

Spain is already the European Union's ‌most fire-affected country this year. According to ​the EU's Copernicus ​wildfire monitoring service, 104,423 hectares had burned across Spain in 2026, compared with 41,781 hectares in France.

The blaze is unfolding after an exceptionally ​destructive fire season ‌last summer, when Spain recorded 354,747 hectares burned and 63 large ​wildfires, the highest annual burned area of the past decade.

(Reporting by ​Emma Pinedo; Editing by Alexandra Hudson)

title: Why the Spokane wildfires exploded so fast: drought, heat and a rare fire warning
content:
Firefighters have gained ground on the three wildfires that destroyed hundreds of buildings around Spokane, Wash., though officials say the threat has not passed.

A man was arrested Monday on suspicion of starting one of the three fires. Aaron F. Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, now faces five counts of first-degree arson. Prosecutors added four after he told detectives he had lit about 25 fires in his neighborhood since July 2025. Investigators verified four of them.

The added counts cover the Aubrey White fire, which burned more than 1,200 acres in July 2025; a second blaze two days later within five miles of it; the Equestrian Fire that August; and the Indian Bluff Fire last month. Prosecutors said the charges "may be further amended as the full extent of the defendant's criminal acts becomes known."

Advertisement Advertisement

Court documents say he began planning the Old Trails Fire about two weeks out, using a weather app to pick a day with high wind, low humidity and heat, and settled on Aug. 1. He also studied the methods of other arsonists, including John Leonard Orr, and bought materials to build what the affidavit calls a "time delay device."

"He feels fire is powerful, beautiful, and that things that go through fire experience a kind of rebirth," wrote one of the detectives who interviewed him.

Farinacci did not enter a plea at his arraignment Thursday. His attorney requested a competency evaluation, and the judge raised his bond to $2 million. His next hearing is Sept. 4.

Court records show Farinacci has a history of mental health problems.

Advertisement Advertisement

Farinacci shot and killed his adoptive father, Jeffrey Farinacci, at their home in Mesa, Ariz., in October 2010 after an argument over dishes, the Associated Press reported, citing records. Court documents say he took a .22-caliber pistol from a closet and fired twice as his father came through a bedroom door. He then ran from the house and shot himself in the chest.

The dispute went beyond the dishes, according to court records reviewed by NBC News. Farinacci described his father "slapping him around, cornered him and was in his face." He gave investigators shifting accounts of the shooting itself, saying at various points that his father barged in, that the gun went off accidentally and that he fired in self-defense.

A grand jury charged him with first-degree murder. Before sentencing, a court-ordered psychological evaluation found his intelligence was below average and documented severe anxiety, chronic depression and repeated suicide attempts, NBC reported. It also flagged signs of bipolar disorder and several psychiatric hospitalizations.

He pleaded guilty in 2012 to manslaughter and aggravated assault, drawing 12 years in prison and three years of probation. A sentencing memo said he "hopes to learn appropriate skills while in prison to deal with his anger issues." Arizona corrections records show he was released Dec. 23, 2020.

Advertisement Advertisement

He moved to Washington in 2022 and remained on probation until 2024. He had been staying at his adoptive mother's apartment in Spokane, unemployed and dealing with depression, someone close to the family told NBC News. He has a 16-month-old son.

Last summer, law enforcement contacted Farinacci about two Washington fires, including one investigators called suspicious that started near his home, according to the affidavit. Neither case led to charges.

Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels credited local residents with helping authorities identify the suspect.

"As it happens in so many critical cases, it was citizens who were paying attention to their surroundings, being aware and willing to step up and say something that led to the relatively quick apprehension of Mr. Farinacci," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Officials have not said what may have caused the other two fires.

A statewide emergency was declared on Aug. 1. More than 67,000 people had been ordered to evacuate as of Tuesday, with the first orders issued Aug. 1.

Spokane Mayor Lisa Brown called it "the worst natural disaster our region has faced."

The county initially received nearly 300 reports of missing people, but later cleared all but 14.

What's burning?

The Autumn Lane Fire near Nine Mile Falls is the largest of the three, at 5,783 acres and 47% contained as of Saturday evening. The Old Trails Fire north of Airway Heights had burned 3,561 acres and was 43% contained. The Fairview Fire near Mead is the smallest, at 992 acres and 31% contained. Together they have burned about 10,300 acres since igniting Aug. 1.

"Hundreds of people have completely lost their homes and farms, and many are prohibited from returning to their homes or neighborhoods as crews continue to extinguish smoldering embers," the state's congressional delegation wrote Monday when asking President Donald Trump to approve an expedited emergency declaration.

Advertisement Advertisement

Fire officials estimate the three fires have damaged or destroyed more than 900 structures, most of them in the path of the Old Trails Fire.

The fires near Spokane are three of a total of 13 major wildfires burning across the state of Washington. The largest of the blazes, the Kaiser Canyon Fire, has burned more than 136,000 acres, but it's not located near a major population center.

So far in 2026, Washington has dealt with more than 600 wildfires, which have burned a total of 336,000 acres.

"This year has already been one of our busiest wildfire years on record, and we just started August," Public Lands Commissioner Dave Upthegrove said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Some Spokane residents have returned to find their homes leveled by wildfires that erupted across a parched landscape, covering yards in charred debris. In some cases, only chimneys were left standing.

"There's nothing to save," Miriam Sim, 76, said Monday as she and her husband, Daniel Sim, surveyed the ruins of the home where they had lived since 2005.

"At our age, do we want to rebuild?" her husband asked.

Karen Faggioli, 61, told the Associated Press that she figured she would be returning to her home, but a relative told her that her house and three vehicles were destroyed.

"Why cry? What's crying going to do? I've been through so many tragedies myself," said Faggioli, who is recovering from breast cancer. "This is nothing. Like I told my granddaughter, 'We're strong — and now we get all new things.' I'm emotionally numb."

Advertisement Advertisement

According to the Washington State Department of Natural Resources (DNR) burn ban map, fire restrictions are in effect across much of Washington state.

Ash Sollie looks at her grandparents' house, where she previously lived, after it was destroyed by a wildfire. (Reuters / REUTERS)

Burn bans cover most counties in western and central Washington and extend into several counties in the east, indicating that restrictions have been implemented across a broad geographic area.

Weather changes fast. Get real-time alerts for your area on the new Yahoo Weather app.

Why they spread so fast

Forecasters had warned for days that conditions were primed for disaster.

The National Weather Service issued a "Particularly Dangerous Situation" fire-weather warning for central and eastern Washington for the duration of Aug. 1, a rare step reserved for the most extreme conditions. The Spokesman-Review reported it was the first such warning ever issued for eastern Washington.

Advertisement Advertisement

The trigger was a combination of extreme heat, low humidity and wind gusts of 35 to 45 mph, on top of Washington's fourth straight year of statewide drought. When the Old Trails Fire started near Airway Heights around noon Aug. 1, the wind drove it into Riverside State Park and then across the Spokane River into the city's neighborhoods within hours.

The damage and evacuations

Authorities in Spokane issued evacuation orders on Aug. 1, emptying much of the city's northwest.

Spokane County Commissioner Chris Jordan said on Aug. 2 relatives of his were in an area affected by the fires and didn't know if their home was still standing. He said he spoke with them as they were leaving the home.

"They're in their car and all they can see is smoke everywhere, and it was incredibly scary for so many people," he said during a news conference.

Advertisement Advertisement

The evacuation footprint has shrunk, with the remaining Level 2 and Level 3 zones — seen in yellow and red — more tightly concentrated around the Old Trails Fire near Country Homes and Riverside State Park.

Jana Jensen surveys the neighborhood where her childhood home, owned by her parents, was lost to wildfire, while embracing her son, Aaren, 8. (REUTERS / REUTERS)

What's next

More than 150 agencies have sent crews, and roughly 2,000 firefighters are now assigned to the fires, including teams from a dozen states and Australia.

None of the three fires grew Friday. Crews spent the day testing lines against the first of the two days officials had called the most dangerous stretch of the fire fight. The warning, issued for very low humidity and winds gusting to 25 mph, expired at 11 p.m. Saturday, and forecasters expect conditions to ease.

Hazardous materials teams are assessing neighborhoods still under Level 3 "Go Now" orders. Officials also warn about ash pits and trees weakened by fire, which remain a danger to residents and crews.

title: Bertha’s gone, but its moisture isn’t. Southeast remains on alert for flash floods
author: Dakota Smith
content:
Bertha has fizzled out, but moisture linked to the former tropical storm is still fueling a flood threat that could linger into the weekend for some.

Bertha dissipated over Texas on Thursday evening, where it had little impact except some locally heavy rain, including around Houston.

🌀 ⛈️ Get your storm forecast in the CNN Weather app

The system could have more of an impact farther east, where a plume of its moisture is getting snagged on a slow-moving front. That front has now gone from slow-moving to stalled, locking in rainfall over parts of the Southeast.

Thunderstorms ramped up Friday afternoon across northern Alabama and Georgia and dumped 1 to 2 inches of rain, prompting several flash flood warnings including in Birmingham, Alabama and Atlanta.

A Level 2 of 4 risk of flooding rainfall stretches across the coastal Carolinas to as far inland as Sumter, South Carolina and Fayetteville, North Carolina.

The region needs rain to quench widespread severe to extreme drought, but if it falls too quickly — at rates of 2 inches or more per hour — it could overwhelm the dry ground.

Rainfall totals could reach 4 inches or more in spots, which is the majority of a month’s worth of rain for some. Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, averages 5.40 inches in July.

Other parts of the Southeast could also see rainfall heavy enough to trigger some flooding on Saturday. A Level 1 of 4 risk of flooding rainfall encompasses a large area from western South Carolina to parts of the lower Mississippi Valley.

Bertha’s impacts this week

The flood threat has been in place since Wednesday, when Bertha’s moisture began funneling into the Southeast and southern Virginia in earnest. On Wednesday morning, storms caused flash flooding north of Knoxville, Tennessee, after up to 5 inches of rain fell in a few hours.

Flash flood warnings were issued in North Carolina, including Greensboro and Winston-Salem, Wednesday night, where heavy storms dropped up to 6 inches of rain — a month’s worth — in 12 hours. There were no flood reports from the area, where a serious drought and prolonged, rather than intense, rainfall helped mitigate the threat.

On Thursday morning, flooding temporarily closed a short section of Interstate 40 northwest of Durham, North Carolina, according to the state’s department of transportation.

As for Bertha itself, it proved to mostly be a nuisance this week along the Gulf Coast, from the Florida Panhandle to Texas.

Unfavorable winds in the atmosphere kept the tropical storm lopsided, with much of its heaviest rain and strongest winds over the Gulf instead of land. Dangerous beach conditions and minor coastal flooding were the main impacts along the northern Gulf Coast.

Vehicles partially buried in sand on Dauphin Island, Alabama, after coastal flooding hit the area earlier this week. Aaron Rigsby / CorClips

Bertha made its first landfall in southeast Louisiana on Wednesday afternoon. Wind gusts over 40 mph were clocked at New Orleans Lakefront Airport.

The storm then skirted farther west along the Louisiana coast before pushing ashore for its final time near the Texas-Louisiana border on Thursday afternoon.

Residents walk in the floodwaters along Lake Pontchartrain in New Orleans as Tropical Storm Bertha approaches the Louisiana coast on Wednesday, July 22. Gerald Herbert/AP

Bertha was the second named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season, which has gotten off to a slow start compared to recent years as El Niño tightens its grip on parts of the basin.

title: Fifth heatwave of the year likely next week as temperatures could hit 35C
content:
Temperatures on Saturday will begin to climb above average again, reaching the mid- to high 20s Celsius in most of England and Wales.

It will be cooler in Scotland and Northern Ireland at 17 to 21C with more cloud, a bit of rain and a blustery wind.

By Sunday and into next week temperatures will rise even further with many parts of the UK exceeding their heatwave threshold temperature of 25 to 28C, depending on location.

With this hotter weather expected to last well into the week, many locations will have the three consecutive days needed to declare the fifth widespread heatwave of the year.

It has already been a remarkable summer in the United Kingdom with multiple records broken.

July has been the sunniest month on record for the UK, as well as the driest July on record for England and Wales.

There have so far been 33 days this year when temperatures have exceeded 30C in the UK. Next week, it is likely the record of 34 days, set in 1995, will be broken.

For the first time ever, a temperature of 35C has also been recorded somewhere in the UK on the three consecutive months of May, June and July.

It is possible August will join that list by the end of next week as some forecast models suggest 35C in central and south-east England.

title: Temperatures to drop briefly ahead of next UK heatwave
content:
Temperatures are set to drop across the UK over the next few days, ending the latest heatwave that has affected some areas of southern and eastern England.

Humidity levels will fall too, which should cool down homes and make nights more comfortable for sleeping.

The change in conditions follows another historic day in a summer that has seen many long standing heat records toppled or tied. On Tuesday, the UK registered its 34th day of temperatures reaching 30C (86F) or higher in a calendar year, equalling the record set in 1995.

Forecasts suggest that this record is likely to be beaten as early as next week, with some showing the potential for a sixth heatwave to develop.

title: Magnitude 7.1 earthquake rocks Japan as tsunami warning issued
author: Abc News
content:
Two women were confirmed dead at a shopping center, local media reported.

13 dead after powerful earthquake rocks Japan, damaging buildings and mall in south: Broadcaster

The damaged AEON Mall after an earthquake in Kashima, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan, July 28, 2026.

The damaged AEON Mall after an earthquake in Kashima, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan, July 28, 2026.

The damaged AEON Mall after an earthquake in Kashima, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan, July 28, 2026.

The damaged AEON Mall after an earthquake in Kashima, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan, July 28, 2026.

TOKYO and LONDON -- At least 13 people are dead after a powerful earthquake rocked southern Japan on Tuesday, according to Japan's public broadcaster NHK, citing remarks by the Japanese prime minister.

The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake measured at a magnitude of 6.8 after initially reporting a preliminary magnitude of 7.1.

The quake struck Kyushu Island, in the Kumamoto Prefecture, shortly before 4:30 p.m. local time, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

As of Wednesday morning local time, 13 people have been found dead, Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae said, according to NHK.

At least two people -- two women in their 20s -- died at a shopping center that partially collapsed according to local authorities and broadcasters.

Aerials taken above the shopping mall appeared to show that several walls, as well as the roof, partially collapsed. NHK reported that the fire department said the building's second floor collapsed.

The Fire and Disaster Management Agency said many people could be trapped inside the mall, NHK reported.

The damaged AEON Mall after an earthquake in Kashima, Kumamoto prefecture, southern Japan, July 28, 2026. Kyodo News via AP

The shopping mall was evacuated when the quake struck, NHK News reported, adding that there appeared to have been an explosion in the earthquake's aftermath.

Rescue operations at the mall were ongoing in the wake of the earthquake, according to police.

The quake struck about 6 miles beneath the island, which is the southernmost of the main Japanese islands, according to local and U.S. weather officials.

The quake prompted the Japan Meteorological Agency to issue and later lift a tsunami advisory for the coasts of the Ariake Sea and the Yatsushiro Sea.

The agency warned that further quakes may strike the area in the coming days, with an official saying, "As the place where the latest earthquake occurred is shallow, this shows that many earthquakes have occurred."

“We have already confirmed extensive damage, including casualties, collapsed buildings, damaged roads and fires," Takaichi said during a task force emergency response meeting in Tokyo on Tuesday.

Reporters watch the news showing a large quake and possible one meter tsunami wave in Southern Japan, from an office in Tokyo on July 28, 2026. Andrew Caballero-reynolds/AFP via Getty Images

The rumbling on Tuesday afternoon lasted for about a minute, according to NHK News, which broadcast images of apparent smoke or fire nearby.

The prefecture's airport, Kumamoto Airport, in Mashiki, suspended all flights shortly after the quake, according to a notice posted on its website.

A task force for emergency disaster response was created Tuesday, headed by Takaichi, she said. Self-defense forces with approximately 3,600 personnel began operations in affected areas, according to the prime minister.

The exterior wall of a shop is seen collapsed in an earthquake, in Kumamoto City on July 28, 2026. JIJI Press/AFP via Getty Images

Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority said in an emergency update that it had not recorded "abnormalities" at nearby facilities in Ikata, Genkai and Satsumasendai City.

Several thousand homes were without power following the quake, NHK reported.

Officials urged people to stay away from the ocean and the seashore. They also warned residents to watch for possible landslides.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaks to the media at the Prime Minister's Office, in Tokyo after a 7.1-magnitude earthquake hit southern Japan on July 28, 2026. JIJI Press/AFP via Getty Images

Takaichi said strong shaking could be felt in both city of Uki and the town of Hikawa. She warned of potential tsunamis of about a meter, or just over 3 feet, near the Ariake and Yatsushiro seas.

“To those in areas that experienced strong shaking, the risk of building collapses and landslides remains high," Takaichi said. "Please avoid entering dangerous areas and take all precautions to ensure your safety."

The prime minister urged residents to remain alert for possible earthquakes over the next week or so, which she said could reach a seismic intensity of 7.

ABC News' Joe Simonetti contributed to this report.

title: The Papers: '45m Brits in drought' and a 'Not-so-small boats crisis'
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
Many of the papers lead on the arrival of a record 230 migrants on a single 49ft dinghy. The Daily Mail, external notes the number is more than the capacity of a Boeing-737 and says the small boats crisis has become a "big boats crisis". The Sun, external takes a similar approach with its headline, "not-so-small boats crisis". It says the crossing will cost taxpayers £25m. The Daily Telegraph, external carries a warning from the French lifeboat service, which says there is "no limit" to the number of migrants people smugglers will put on board the giant dinghies.

Andy Burnham's call for the justice secretary to draw up plans to exclude PC Harper's killers from the prison early release scheme leads the Times, external. A government source is quoted in the report, saying the prime minister never accepted that Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers should walk free.

The Daily Mirror, external reports on the drought conditions for most of Britain under the headline, "high and dry". The paper says 45 million people are now in drought areas. The Guardian, external says firefighters have warned they aren't properly equipped to deal with what they call an "unprecedented" surge in wildfires as a result of the dry conditions. According to the report, the Fire Brigades Union says ensuring crews are prepared to tackle the rising threat should be a "national priority".

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has told the Daily Express, external that Andy Burnham needs to rule out further tax rises to fund his new policies. Writing in the paper, she says the prime minister and his new chancellor, John Healey, face a "tricky test" in the Budget. In response, Labour says it will focus on problem solving, not point scoring.

The Financial Times, external leads on what it calls one of Wall Street's most ambitious lending efforts. It says some of the largest financial groups are working on a five hundred billion dollar package with the artificial intelligence firm, Nvidia, to invest in AI data centres.

"You'll never deliver alone" reads the Daily Star's, external headline with the paper reporting on the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, nearing a deal to buy a stake in Liverpool football club. Its front page features a picture of a Liverpool player with the billionaire's face edited on.
